after.asserts:
Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions with finite VC dimension $d$, put $\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$, and let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathcal Z$. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a map $A:\mathcal Z^m\to H$ for which $S\mapsto R_P(A(S))$ and $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(A(S))$ are measurable, where
$$R_P(h):=P\{(x,y):h(x)\ne y\},\qquad \widehat R_S(h):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{h(X_i)\ne Y_i\}.$$
Suppose $P$ is realizable by $H$ and $A$ is consistent $P^m$-almost surely. For $0<\epsilon<1$, assume the events
$$E_{m,\epsilon}:=\{S\in\mathcal Z^m:\exists h\in H,\ R_P(h)>\epsilon,\ \widehat R_S(h)=0\}$$
and
$$B_{m,\epsilon}:=\{(S,S')\in\mathcal Z^m\times\mathcal Z^m:\exists h\in H,\ R_P(h)>\epsilon,\ \widehat R_S(h)=0,\ \widehat R_{S'}(h)\ge\epsilon/2\}$$
are measurable in their respective product sigma-algebras; this holds when $H$ is countable. For $0<\epsilon,\delta<1$ and $S\sim P^m$, if $d=0$ then $R_P(A(S))=0$ almost surely for every such rule. If $d\ge1$ and
$$m\ge\frac{64}{\epsilon}\left[d\log\!\left(\frac{64e}{\epsilon}\right)+\log\!\left(\frac4\delta\right)\right],$$
where $\log$ is natural and $e=\exp(1)$, then $\mathbb P\{R_P(A(S))\le\epsilon\}\ge1-\delta$. This is a conditional upper bound for consistent risk-measurable learners; it asserts no existence or computational-efficiency result.

Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets of feature types and score bins. For each group $t\in\{1,2\}$, let $N_t>0$ be its total mass and let $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}=1$. Let $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ be the probability of the positive binary outcome $Y=1$ for feature type $\sigma$, with the same $p_\sigma$ in both groups. A randomized risk assignment consists of scores $v_b\in[0,1]$ for $b\in\mathcal B$ and a single matrix $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$ with $\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}X_{\sigma b}=1$ for each $\sigma$; conditional on feature type $\sigma$, the assignment chooses bin $b$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}$, independently of group and outcome. Thus, for a group-$t$ individual chosen according to its feature distribution, $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=1,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}$ and $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=0,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}$, and the assigned score is $S=v_B$. The expected positive mass is $\mu_t=N_t\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$, and the group base rate is $\rho_t=\mu_t/N_t$.

The assignment is **calibrated within group $t$** if for every $b\in\mathcal B$,
$$
\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}=v_b\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}X_{\sigma b}.
$$

In group $t$, feature type $\sigma$ has proportion $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$, where $\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}=1$, and total mass $N_t>0$. The positive binary outcome $Y=1$ has probability $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ for feature type $\sigma$, with the same $p_\sigma$ in both groups. $$

The constant utility $u(D,a)=1$, $u(D,b)=0$ has $\Delta_u=0$, so it is inadmissible for the positive-sensitivity exponential mechanism. Fix a possible record $u_*\in U$ and define $s(D)=1$ exactly when $D(u_*)>0$. Instead set $u(D,a)=1$ and $u(D,b)=1-s(D)$. Then $\Delta_u=1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,0)$-differentially private, and it selects $a$ with probability
$$
\frac{e^{\varepsilon/2}}{e^{\varepsilon/2}+e^{\varepsilon(1-s(D))/2}}.
$$

after.asserts:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, fix $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, and choose $\sigma_{\min}>0$. Let $Z$ have the standard multivariate normal law $N_d(0,I_d)$. For $t\in[0,1]$, define
$$\mu_t(x_1):=t x_1,\qquad \sigma_t:=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad \psi_t(z\mid x_1):=\sigma_t z+\mu_t(x_1),$$
and let $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ be the law of $\psi_t(Z\mid x_1)$. Then $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is the Gaussian probability path with mean $\mu_t(x_1)$ and covariance $\sigma_t^2I_d$, and its Lebesgue density is
$$\rho_t(x\mid x_1)=(2\pi\sigma_t^2)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x-\mu_t(x_1)\|_2^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right).$$
A conditional velocity field for this path is
$$u_t(x\mid x_1)=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}(x-tx_1)+x_1.$$
For each endpoint $x_1$, these densities and fields form a conditional path in the probability-path definition; hence they can be mixed against any Borel endpoint law. At $t=0$ the law is $N_d(0,I_d)$, and at $t=1$ it is the law of $x_1+\sigma_{\min}Z$, a Gaussian with mean $x_1$ and covariance $\sigma_{\min}^2I_d$. The affine endpoint map $T(z)=x_1+\sigma_{\min}z$ is optimal for squared Euclidean cost between these two laws: every coupling has cost at least
$$\|x_1\|_2^2+d(1-\sigma_{\min})^2,$$
and the law of $(Z,T(Z))$ attains this value.

after.asserts:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $a\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma_{\min}>0$, let $Z\sim N(0,1)$, and set
$$\sigma_t=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad X_t=\sigma_t Z+ta\quad(0\le t\le1).$$
Then $X_t\sim N(ta,\sigma_t^2)$, with density
$$\rho_t(x\mid a)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_t}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right),$$
and a conditional velocity field is
$$u_t(x\mid a)=a+\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}(x-ta).$$
For every fixed $z\in\mathbb R$, the particle path $t\mapsto\sigma_tz+ta$ is a straight line from $z$ to $a+\sigma_{\min}z$. The endpoint map $T(z)=a+\sigma_{\min}z$ is quadratic-cost optimal from $N(0,1)$ to $N(a,\sigma_{\min}^2)$, and its squared transport cost is $a^2+(1-\sigma_{\min})^2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix $a>0$ and $\sigma_{\min}>0$. Let the endpoint law assign probability $1/2$ to each endpoint $x_1=-a$ and $x_1=a$. For each endpoint, use the one-dimensional Gaussian path with
$$\sigma_t=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad X_t=\sigma_t Z+t x_1,\qquad Z\sim N(0,1).$$
For either endpoint and each fixed $Z=z$, the conditional particle trajectory is a straight line. The marginal density is
$$p_t(x)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_t}\left[ \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right)+ \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x+ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right) \right],$$
and its marginal velocity field, defined by averaging the conditional velocity against the endpoint density at fixed $(t,x)$, is
$$u^m_t(x)=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}x+ \frac{a}{\sigma_t}\tanh\!\left(\frac{atx}{\sigma_t^2}\right), \qquad \tanh(y):=\frac{\exp(y)-\exp(-y)}{\exp(y)+\exp(-y)}.$$
The denominator in the definition of $\tanh$ is positive for every real input. The density is strictly positive, and $\partial_tp_t(x)+\partial_x(p_t(x)u^m_t(x))=0$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R$. For every $t\in(0,1)$, $x\mapsto u^m_t(x)$ is nonlinear.

after.asserts: For an integer $K\ge2$, let the label set be $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ and let $\Delta_K=\{q\in[0,1]^K:\sum_{j=1}^Kq_j=1\}$. A finite-label score loss is a function $S:\Delta_K\times\mathcal Y\to[0,+\infty]$ whose section $q\mapsto S(q,j)$ is Borel measurable for every label $j$. If the true label distribution is $p\in\Delta_K$ and the reported forecast is $q\in\Delta_K$, its expected score loss is $\bar S(p,q)=\sum_{j=1}^Kp_jS(q,j)$, where a term with $p_j=0$ contributes zero even when $S(q,j)=+\infty$. The loss is **proper** if $\bar S(p,p)\le\bar S(p,q)$ for every $p,q\in\Delta_K$, and **strictly proper** if equality implies $q=p$. The logarithmic loss is $S_{\log}(q,j)=-\log q_j$, with $-\log0=+\infty$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm; the Brier loss is $S_{\mathrm B}(q,j)=\sum_{i=1}^K(q_i-\mathbf1_{\{i=j\}})^2$.

after.asserts:
Let $K\ge2$, let $Y$ be a random variable into the finite label set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable forecast, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$. The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

Let $Y\in\{-1,+1\}$ be the label in a supervised prediction problem with the full power-set sigma-algebra on this binary label set, and choose the finite-label conditional probability function ordered as $(-1,+1)$; write $\eta(x)=\eta_{+1}(x)$. Let $\Phi:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ be finite, convex and nondecreasing. It is continuous on $\mathbb R$; extend it to $\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$ by its one-sided monotone limits, which may equal $+\infty$. The resulting extended function is Borel measurable. For $u\in\overline{\mathbb R}$ define the conditional margin risk
$$L_\Phi(x,u)=\eta(x)\Phi(-u)+(1-\eta(x))\Phi(u),$$
using $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ at endpoints. A measurable extended-real conditional minimizer is a measurable $h_\Phi^*:\mathsf X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ satisfying $L_\Phi(x,h_\Phi^*(x))\le L_\Phi(x,u)$ for every $x$ and every $u\in\overline{\mathbb R}$. For a measurable real-valued score $h$, its margin loss is $\ell_\Phi(h(x),y)=\Phi(-yh(x))$, its surrogate risk is $L_\Phi(h)=\mathbb E[\Phi(-Yh(X))]$, and its conditional-minimum risk is $L_\Phi^*=\mathbb E[L_\Phi(X,h_\Phi^*(X))]$. Under the zero-score-is-error convention, its classification risk is $R_{01}(h)=P(Yh(X)\le0)$, and the Bayes classification risk is $R_{01}^*=\mathbb E[\min\{\eta(X),1-\eta(X)\}]$. Write $h^*(x)=\eta(x)-\tfrac12$ for the centered conditional class probability.

Let $Y$ be a random variable into $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra, $K\ge2$, and let $G\in\Delta_K$ be a random forecast with measurable calibration function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$. Let $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and satisfy $d(p,p)=0$. For a finite data-independent Borel partition $\mathcal P$ of $\Delta_K$, draw an iid sequence $(G_i,Y_i)$ from the joint law of $(G,Y)$, let $V_i=e_{Y_i}$ be the corresponding standard basis vector, and form the empirical estimator
$$\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P}=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\frac{N_B}{n}\,d(\bar V_B,\bar G_B),$$
where $N_B=\#\{i\le n:G_i\in B\}$ and, when $N_B>0$, $\bar V_B$ and $\bar G_B$ are the sample averages in bin $B$; when $N_B=0$, set both to any fixed $q_0\in\Delta_K$. Define
$$E_{\mathcal P}=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P:P(G\in B)>0}P(G\in B)\,d\!\left(\mathbb E[r(G)\mid G\in B],\mathbb E[G\mid G\in B]\right).$$
For each fixed $\mathcal P$, $\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P}\to E_{\mathcal P}$ almost surely. If $d$ is additionally jointly convex, then $E_{\mathcal P}\le\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$. Without requiring convexity, if $\mathcal P_m$ is a sequence of finite data-independent Borel partitions whose mesh $\max_{B\in\mathcal P_m}\operatorname{diam}_2(B)$ tends to zero, where $\operatorname{diam}_2(B)=\sup_{u,v\in B}\|u-v\|_2$, and $r$ is Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean metric on $\Delta_K$, then $E_{\mathcal P_m}\to\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$. Thus the iterated limit $\lim_{m\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P_m}$ equals the expected calibration error almost surely; no diagonal rate is asserted.

Fix $K\ge2$. The input is a trained classifier with a measurable, finite-valued
logit map $z:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$, a nonempty finite validation sample
$(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n_v}$ with $n_v\ge1$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and a
finite nonempty set of candidate temperatures $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$.
The validation labels were not used to fit the logits. For $T\in\mathcal T$,
compute
$$p_T(j\mid x)=\frac{\exp(z_j(x)/T)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell(x)/T)}\quad (j=1,\ldots,K),\qquad L_{\mathrm{val}}(T)=-\frac1{n_v}\sum_{i=1}^{n_v}\log p_T(y_i\mid x_i).$$

$$T^*=\min\arg\min_{T\in\mathcal T}L_{\mathrm{val}}(T).$$
and return the forecasts $p_{T^*}(\cdot\mid x)$ and predicted label
$\min\arg\max_j p_{T^*}(j\mid x)$ for each input $x$. This is a
finite-candidate version of validation negative-log-likelihood temperature
scaling. It selects only by empirical validation loss; it makes no finite-sample
calibration guarantee for future data, particularly when the validation and
future data laws differ.

after.asserts:
Fix a prompt $q$, a parameter $\theta$ in the open domain of its finite response policy, a finite real reward function $r$ on the policy support, and an integer $G\ge2$. Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_G$ be independent responses with common law $\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid q)$, let $R_i:=r(Y_i)$, let $S_i:=\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(Y_i\mid q)$, and set
$\overline R:=G^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{G}R_j$ and $J(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[r(Y)\mid q]$.
Then
$$\mathbb E_\theta\left[\frac1G\sum_{i=1}^{G}(R_i-\overline R)S_i\mid q\right]=\left(1-\frac1G\right)\nabla_\theta J(\theta).$$
If instead $\overline R_{-i}:=(G-1)^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}R_j$, then
$$\mathbb E_\theta\left[\frac1G\sum_{i=1}^{G}(R_i-\overline R_{-i})S_i\mid q\right]=\nabla_\theta J(\theta).$$
